title: With the Samanas

teacherSummary.text: With the Samanas, Siddhartha learns fasting, enduring pain, and meditations that let his self pass into animals and objects. Yet after three years he concludes these are only escapes from the self, not true release. When rumors spread of Gotama, the Buddha, he and Govinda leave; Siddhartha masters the old Samana with his gaze before departing.

items.prompt: Siddhartha compares the Samanas’ meditation to the carter’s rice wine (paragraph 13). Govinda answers that the two are not alike. Who has the stronger case? Argue one side and answer the other.
items.author: r12-handwritten
items.expected: Govinda’s reply is an argument from results, and the chapter’s evidence answers it. Siddhartha calls the exercises “a short numbing of the senses against the pain and the pointlessness of life” (With the Samanas, paragraph 13), the same thing the oxcart driver finds in rice wine. Govinda grants the numbing but denies that the outcome is the same: the drinker will “return from the delusion, finds everything to be unchanged, has not become wiser, has gathered no enlightenment—has not risen several steps” (paragraph 14), which implies that the Samana does rise. That is the right test, a lasting gain, and Siddhartha answers it on Govinda’s own terms. He says that he is “just as far removed from wisdom, from salvation, as a child in the mother’s womb” (paragraph 15), and when Govinda insists that “we have already ascended many a level” (paragraph 17), Siddhartha points to their teacher: “He has lived for sixty years and has not reached the nirvana” (paragraph 20). Siddhartha has the stronger case on the evidence; Govinda’s reply holds only if one trusts a gain that no one around them shows.

items.prompt: Siddhartha leaves his father and the Samanas in very different ways: he waits all night for his father’s consent, but he compels the old Samana with a spell. Does the difference show growth or loss? Argue from both scenes and answer the other reading.
items.author: r11-handwritten
items.expected: The difference reads more as loss than growth. At home he refuses to leave without consent and stands until the father sees that “he had already left him” (The Son of the Brahmin, paragraph 47); his will wins, but by patience, and the blessing is given freely. contentNotes.teacherNote: Among the worldly sights Siddhartha rejects are “whores offering themselves” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Samanas, para. 2), and he speaks of “In every tavern of that part of a town where the whorehouses are, my friend, among carters and gamblers I could have learned it.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Samanas, para. 11). These are crude, insulting words for sex workers and brothels (places where sex is sold), not slurs; today say “sex workers” or “brothel.” They show his contempt for city life. The chapter also shows ascetic self-punishment, framed as religious practice that the novel judges a dead end: “It is fleeing from the self, it is a short escape of the agony of being a self, it is a short numbing of the senses against the pain and the pointlessness of life.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Samanas, para. 13) Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.
